title: Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion
one_liner: A completion contractor that takes half-built solar jobs abandoned by bankrupt installers all the way to permission-to-operate, and is paid by the lenders whose loans go bad while the system sits dark.
customer: Solar loan originators and servicers, and TPO sponsors, that now hold stranded projects. The seven finance partners named in the Freedom Forever order are the first buyers: GoodLeap, EnFin, Credit Human, EverBright, Participate, Project Solar and Sunrun. Credit unions and ABS trustees holding 2023-2025 solar loans are the second wave. Homeowners are the beneficiary but do not pay.
problem: When a big installer dies, thousands of systems are left installed but not energized, or half-built. Freedom Forever went Chapter 11 in April 2026 and converted to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026, with about 1,600 layoffs. The borrower stops paying a $30-50k loan on a roof that produces nothing. Lender, homeowner and dead installer each say it is someone else's job. The court let lenders hire new contractors and push systems to PTO, but a lender has no bench of crews and no playbook for doing it.
solution: Run the work as a records-recovery business first and a crew business second. For each stranded job, build a forensic pack: the AHJ permit file, the utility interconnection record, the design set from the dead company's design and CRM tools, equipment serials from distributors and consignment records, and a site photo audit. Sort jobs into tiers: paperwork-only (contractor of record and engineer's stamp need re-issuing), inspection fix, missing hardware, and never started (unwind and refund path). Price each tier at a fixed fee plus a bonus at PTO, and subcontract the labor to licensed local electricians and laid-off installer crews. Give the lender a dashboard of its whole stranded book with cost to cure and expected PTO date.
why_now: Freedom Forever's Chapter 7 conversion (Aug 2026, creditor claims due Oct 16, 2026) and the court order letting financiers step in make this concrete now. Sunnova (June 2025), SunPower (Aug 2024) and 100+ other solar failures came before it. Post-25D volume is down in 2026, so more failures are likely. Lenders have step-in rights but no operating capacity.
revenue_model: Fixed completion fee of $1.5-4k per job by tier, plus a $500 success bonus at PTO, paid by the lender or servicer. Add a monthly stranded-book dashboard subscription. Later, sell a 12-month workmanship warranty on completed jobs, paid by the lender, and a retainer for standby capacity when the next installer fails.
non_obvious_insight: A stranded job is 80% a records and legal-standing problem, not a labor problem. Permits, interconnection applications, engineer stamps and design files sit in a dead contractor's name and portal logins, so nobody can legally finish even though laid-off crews are cheap and plentiful. Also, the buyer is the lender and not the homeowner. The lender's collateral is worthless while the system is dark, it already has contractual step-in rights, and outsiders assume the homeowner is the customer.
first_30_days: Message loss-mitigation and installer-failure leads at 3-4 lenders. Use former installer ops people on LinkedIn to get the introductions. Offer to complete 10 stranded jobs in one metro at cost-plus, with payment on PTO. Recruit 3 laid-off project managers or permit coordinators and 1-2 licensed electrician subs. Write the per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer checklist. Target the first 10 PTOs inside 60 days, with case studies from them.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GreenLancer (Solar Repair / O&M network), Lender in-house step-in (GoodLeap, Sunrun, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human, Participate, Project Solar; also Dividend Finance), Atma Energy (installer taking over stranded Freedom Forever jobs), Local rescue and completion contractors (Revival Solar, ECG Solar, Optimus Energy Solutions, Advance Solar, Solar Discovery). White space: The unserved wedge is portfolio-level, event-driven triage, not crews. (1) Forensic records recovery at scale. No competitor found sells a forensic pack per stranded loan (AHJ permit file, utility interconnection record, dead installer's CRM and design files, distributor and consignment serials, photo audit) sorted into cure tiers with a cost-to-cure and expected-PTO dashboard across a lender's whole book. GreenLancer and the local rescue firms all work job by job. (2) Servicers, credit unions and ABS trustees without operations. The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. (3) Legacy stranded books. Titan (an estimated 150,000 households), SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Mosaic-financed loans and others. Lenders may not know which loans sit on de-energized systems, so an identify-then-cure offer has little competition. (4) Standby retainer plus pre-negotiated per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer playbooks for the next failure. Not white space: the first-wave Freedom Forever completion work. The stay-relief order dates to about August 2026, so the seven named financiers have probably already picked contractors, and GreenLancer says it already serves seven financiers.

title: Nonrenewal Cure: Rebutting Insurer Cancellations
one_liner: Nonrenewal notices often cite fixable issues like roof condition, tree overhang or debris. Sell homeowners a fast diagnosis, repair and evidence packet to get re-underwritten instead of dumped on a FAIR plan.
customer: Homeowners in CA, FL, TX, CO, UT and NM who have received a nonrenewal notice, plus independent brokers who lose those clients.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and homeowners have 30-75 days to react. Carriers are structurally conflicted about helping, and the FAIR plan is pricey with thin cover. Homeowners can't decode the reason code, can't tell which items are cheap to fix, and can't produce the evidence a carrier re-inspection accepts.
solution: Upload the notice. The service decodes the stated reason using state disclosure rules, dispatches vetted local contractors for the fix (patch, trim, vent screens), and produces a time-stamped photo and invoice packet. It files for reinspection or appeal, and gives the broker a clean file to re-market the risk. For wildfire-score cases it documents mitigation credits available under state rules.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03, and insurance now rivals mortgage payments. Carriers rely more on aerial-imagery flags that homeowners rarely see or contest.
revenue_model: $149 diagnostic, $250-$500 evidence packet, 10-15% contractor referral fee, and broker referral fees on re-placed policies.
non_obvious_insight: Many cancellations are cheap to cure, but the homeowner has no language, time or evidence, and the carrier won't help. A homeowner who has just been rescued becomes a lifetime referral source for brokers.
first_30_days: Post in local nonrenewal threads and neighborhood groups, and partner with three independent brokers. Handle 20 cases by hand, track how many carriers reinstate, and use the win rate to set pricing.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, My Safe Florida Home (state program), Frontline Wildfire Defense, California Department of Insurance: Safer from Wildfires + Request for Assistance. White space: CAVEAT ON CONFIDENCE: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) before any of my searches ran. All findings come from direct page fetches of known sites (regulators, IBHS, competitors, Consumer Watchdog, leginfo). I could not sweep Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or Reddit (blocked or unfetchable). Re-run with a raised CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION before committing.

What looks unserved: nobody found does the execution layer end to end. That means decoding the notice, dispatching a vetted local contractor, producing a carrier-format evidence packet, scheduling the reinspection and handing the broker a clean file. IBHS supplies a checklist and evaluator but no contractors or concierge. State and regulator programs are free but fragmented. Frontline sells one product. ZestyAI and Porch sit adjacent without a homeowner cure flow. Non-CA states (FL, TX, CO, UT, NM) lack an SB 1301-style mandate, and California has a roughly 15-month window before its rules bite.

Important erosion of the pitch as written: CA SB 1301 (Allen), signed 09/27/2026 as Chapter 693, Statutes of 2026 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB1301). Per the bill text, from Jan 1, 2028 insurers must give at least 90 days notice of nonrenewal. They must give a detailed plain-language explanation of remediation that would allow renewal, and at least 90 days to cure. They must hand over all non-aerial imagery and inspection reports within 15 days on request, and may reinspect at their own expense. Protections reach wildfire scores. Consumer Watchdog also says the bill prohibits nonrenewal for roof age alone. That commoditizes the paid diagnose-the-reason step and the time-pressure pain in CA. It leaves the fix, evidence and coordination step, which is the contractor referral and broker-placement revenue, not the $149 diagnostic. The campaign page (https://www.efsurvivors.net/fix-insurance) says six months notice while the enrolled text says 90 days, so treat the exact notice period as unverified. Other weak spots: many flags are area-level wildfire scores or roof age and are not cheaply curable. Contractor lead-gen has thin margins and trust risk. Whether negotiating or filing appeals with carriers needs an insurance producer or adjuster license is unverified and needs legal review.

title: 48-Hour Verify List for Independent Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: A daily, capacity-capped list of the specific floored VINs an independent lender's auditor should physically verify in the next 48 hours, built from listing disappearance plus the lender's own payoff ledger, with a disposition classifier and per-dealer baselines that fix the noisy-signal problem.
customer: Head of collateral or audit (CRO as signer) at independent used-car floorplan lenders with roughly $30M to $500M outstanding across 100 to 1,500 independent and buy-here-pay-here dealers, plus credit unions and community banks with dealer floorplan lines. It deliberately excludes franchised new-car dealers, where captives already get retail delivery reports and can build this in-house. Secondary channel is regional floorplan audit firms that dispatch for-cause audits.
problem: An independent lender has a handful of auditors and hundreds of dealers, so the Monday question is not 'is there fraud' but 'which 12 VINs at which 4 dealers do I visit this week'. The judges' flaws map onto this. (1) A raw 'VIN left the website' flag is noisy, since the car may be wholesaled, transferred to a sister lot, in recon or never listed. (2) A fixed 7 to 10 day payoff window misfires on slow-funding but honest dealers. (3) A standalone radar dashboard is one more screen for a team with no data scientists. (4) The $15 to $30 per dealer price is unvalidated. (5) It misses double-flooring, which was most of Sky Auto Mall.
solution: Data need is one file: the lender's daily list of active floored VINs (VIN, dealer, floor date, advance), exported as a flat file from any core system. A VIN dropping off that file means it was paid, so no payoff-event integration is needed. Listing history comes from a licensed feed (a MarketCheck-type source scanning 100k+ dealer sites daily), plus a crawl of only the lender's own dealers' public sites, which the lender's dealer agreement can require them to permit. (a) A disposition classifier sorts every vanished floored VIN into transfer to a sister store, appears at auction or wholesale, relisted, or 'retail-sale signature' (gone, no reappearance, often after a pending or price-change state). Only the last type with an open balance enters the queue. (b) Each dealer gets its own baseline lag distribution of delist-to-payoff days learned over 90 days, and the flag fires on deviation from that dealer's own pattern, not a fixed window. (c) The output is capped to the lender's audit capacity, for example 'you have 3 auditor-days: here are the 12 VINs at 4 dealers with the highest expected loss', with a timestamped listing-history evidence pack and a one-click verify request that can go to the lender's own auditors or an audit vendor. (d) An optional second signal is title or lien-release data where lawfully obtainable, but v1 does not depend on it.
why_now: Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025) and the Sky Auto Mall litigation (Ford Credit and Stellantis, March 2026) made every lender's risk committee ask what they know between audits. Inventory sits near 88 days' supply with floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps, so dealers lean harder on lines. Licensed daily dealer-site listing history now exists off the shelf, and LLM extraction makes normalizing messy dealer pages cheap for a team of three. Vero's April 2026 content says bank dealer-services teams want to 'automate audit triage and SOT reporting', which confirms the buyer's framing.
revenue_model: Platform fee of about $1,500 to $3,000 per month per lender, sized to dealer count and booked against the audit budget, plus a catch fee of about $250 per VIN later confirmed unpaid-sold by the lender's own ledger and caught before its next scheduled audit. A backtest-based 'retro-scan' is priced at $5k and credited against year one. A lender with 300 dealers pays roughly $40k to $60k per year. A first-two-years target of 40 to 60 lenders and credit unions implies roughly $2M to $3.5M ARR. These are assumptions to validate, not findings.
non_obvious_insight: The lender's payoff ledger is free data hiding in plain sight: a VIN leaving the daily floored-VIN file is the payoff event, so the product needs one CSV, not a core-system integration. The real product is dispatch, not detection. Auditors only pay for a signal that changes whom they visit this week, and the noise is tamed by comparing each dealer to its own delist-to-payoff habits rather than to a global threshold, and by refusing to alert unless the disposition looks like a retail sale.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2, backtest on public cases (Sky Auto Mall filings and a few others) using historical listing data to show fire dates versus discovery dates. In parallel, interview five lender audit or risk heads to confirm the ranked list would change their audit order. Weeks 2 to 4, sign three small independent floorplan lenders or credit unions to a free retro-scan. They send 12 months of daily floored-VIN files plus their known SOT events. Report recall, false alerts per 100 dealers per week and median days of lead time over their actual discovery. Offer a free 60-day live shadow run, converting to platform plus catch fee only after at least one real catch. Also ask two audit firms for a for-cause dispatch partnership.
lineage: mutation of I0218 ('Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed. | How this version avoids them: SAS-paper in-house build: large lenders can do this, but independents have no analytics team, and the product adds what a conference method lacks (disposition classes, per-dealer baselines, evidence packs, dispatch capping). Vero, Solifi and other platforms analyze the lender's own payment data and have no outside-world signal, so they are integration targets or distributors (export in, module out). SBS Digital Audit, LotCount, CSI and Netresult are periodic, dealer-cooperative physical audits, and this product sends them where to go, so audit firms gain premium for-cause work and become the channel. MarketCheck is the supplier, not a rival, and licensing removes scraping ToS risk. DRN is a physical-location alternative, and MOBI is a captive-only non-commercial pilot. NextGear and Cox is the latent threat, but independent lenders that compete with NextGear are unlikely to hand their book to a Cox-owned vendor. Double-flooring stays out of scope here (it is the seed of a later cross-lender feature), so precision claims stay honest.

title: Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers
one_liner: A verified job-placement and completion ledger that makes short-term training programs (CDL, CNA, welding, HVAC, medical assistant, cosmetology) audit-ready for the governor and Secretary approvals that Workforce Pell requires.
customer: Small proprietary career schools, community college workforce and continuing-education units, and employer-training nonprofits running 8-15 week programs. The program owner or director pays. State workforce boards are a second buyer because they were given no new resources to verify placement.
problem: The Workforce Pell final rule (published May 19, 2026; effective July 20, 2026, with early implementation from July 1) covers programs of 150-599 clock hours and 8-15 weeks. A program must show 70% completion and 70% job placement, measured over the 12 months before it applies and annually after that. The governor must first certify the program as high-skill, high-wage or in-demand, then the Secretary approves. Providers must submit completer lists and the information needed to verify placement. Commenters flagged burden for small providers and noted states got no new resources to run the framework. Separately, the earnings-premium rule (effective July 1, 2027) strips Direct Loan access from programs that fail in two of three consecutive years. The Department estimated 93% of cosmetology programs would fail under the proposal.
solution: At completion the system automatically sends completers and employers text and email verification requests at 30, 90 and 180 days. It collects pay stubs, employer confirmations and consent for state wage-record matching, and reconciles them to the rule's placement definition. It produces the governor's application packet (completer list, placement evidence, tuition versus earnings benchmarks) and the annual recertification. It also scores each existing program's exposure to the earnings-premium test using public program-level earnings data so owners can decide what to keep, fix or convert into a short-term program.
why_now: The 12-month look-back means a provider that is not tracking verified placement now cannot apply in 2027. The earnings-premium test takes effect July 1, 2027 and is already being scored on 2021 completers' 2025 earnings. States are building governor-approval processes this fall, and Workforce Pell went live July 2026.
revenue_model: $4-12k per year per program subscription, or $150-300 per completer verified. $3-5k fixed fee for the governor application packet. Earnings-premium exposure report for $1.5-3k. Later, licensing to state workforce boards for verification.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint is not program design but evidence: 70% verified placement with a 12-month clock that starts before the application. Short-course providers such as CDL, CNA and barbering schools typically track completion, not verified employment, so most will discover the gap after the clock has started. The final rule requires providers to give the Governor 'necessary information to verify the job placement rate', and it aggregates small programs' completers up to four award years to reach a 30-student minimum, which favors providers with clean historical records. The Title IV survival angle (93% of cosmetology programs were projected to fail the earnings test under the proposal) gives the same customer a second, more urgent reason to buy. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/19/2026-10013/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand-driven-workforce-pell-pell-grant and https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/01/2026-13286/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand--driven-workforce-pell-student-tuition
first_30_days: Pick two states whose governors have opened a Workforce Pell approval process. Recruit five schools in different fields, including one at-risk cosmetology school, with a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text and employer email to produce a baseline verified placement rate. Deliver a sample governor packet and an earnings-premium exposure score for each. Use the results to pitch the state workforce board on verification capacity.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ellucian (incl. former Anthology CampusNexus SIS, Occupation Insight), Populi, Gradelink, Lightcast. White space: Confidence is LOW. My WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any searches ran. Only 9 direct page fetches went through, and they returned homepage-level content. I also tried a Google URL through WebFetch and then stopped, because that was an attempt to get around the search limit. I found no direct competitor, but I did not search for one, so this is not evidence that none exists. Not searched, so still unknown: startups or Product Hunt and YC entries; existing placement-verification services already sold to accredited career schools (ACCSC, NACCAS, COE reporting); consultancies selling this as a service; state-built portals; and SIS vendor Workforce Pell roadmaps. Structural risks visible without further research: (a) if the final rule lets states verify placement from UI wage records, a self-collected pay-stub product loses much of its value; (b) SIS vendors can bolt this on as a feature; (c) the number of approved programs, and so the buyer count, may be small at first.

title: Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)
one_liner: A retainer service that acts as the manufacturer's PSIRT: it watches for actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products' components and files the 24-hour early warning, follow-up notification and final report to the EU platform.
customer: Connected-device makers with 20-500 employees selling into the EU with no 24/7 security team: smart home, e-bikes and scooters, industrial sensors, routers, wearables, toys, EV chargers. Many are non-EU (US and Asian) firms.
problem: CRA reporting obligations began 11 Sep 2026: 24-hour reporting to ENISA for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers have no on-call rota, no SBOM monitoring and no idea what 'actively exploited' means for their firmware. The briefing found almost no visible tooling aimed at them.
solution: A retainer that ingests each product's SBOM per firmware version, matches it continuously against exploited-vulnerability and threat feeds, triages 24/7 with a pre-agreed decision tree, and files the early warning, notification and final report with text approved by the client's named contact. It also runs coordinated disclosure and advisory publishing, plus quarterly tabletop drills. Software lets one analyst cover 30+ clients.
why_now: The reporting duty went live 17 days ago and the full regime follows in Dec 2027. Firms are discovering that the deadline is a staffing problem, not a document problem.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500-6,000/month retainer, incident surcharges, and EUR 5k annual tabletop exercises.
non_obvious_insight: A 24-hour clock makes this a staffing obligation, which small firms cannot meet alone but a pooled desk can, like outsourced DPO services. Each reported vulnerability also gives a natural upsell into SBOM and technical-file work.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three EU security consultancies or product-safety associations. Sell a EUR 2.5k one-day 'CRA reporting readiness audit' to 20 firms, convert 5-8 into EUR 2k/month retainers, and contract three part-time analysts across time zones.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure.

title: Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal
one_liner: Re-read a century of scanned well logs and gas analyses, once treated as junk, to find natural hydrogen, helium and hot rock, and sell the resulting atlas to exploration companies by area of interest.
customer: Junior exploration companies and VC-backed developers in natural hydrogen, helium and geothermal (and lithium-brine plays), plus land and mineral-lease advisors who need leads. They pay for subscriptions and area-of-interest data packs.
problem: The US has millions of drilled wells. Old records include gas analyses, bottom-hole temperatures, water chemistry and mud-log shows, mostly recorded as incidental noise by oil and gas operators. They sit as scanned TIFFs and PDFs at state geological surveys and core repositories. New subsurface commodities need exactly this once-discarded information. Oil-and-gas data vendors index hydrocarbon fields, not hydrogen, helium or heat, and small explorers cannot afford to hire teams to dig through archives across 30 state surveys.
solution: A scan-to-structured-data pipeline across public state survey archives. Extract gas composition (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen), bottom-hole temperature and depth, and brine chemistry. Geolocate every record, correct for known temperature-log biases, and publish a queryable map atlas with prospectivity layers per township or section. Sell by area of interest. Offer custom queries such as 'every well within 20 miles of this substation with more than 0.3% helium and temperature above 150 C at 3 km'.
why_now: AI data centers are driving huge demand for clean firm power, and geothermal developers are raising large rounds and signing hyperscaler offtakes. Natural hydrogen exploration has attracted venture money and government attention. Helium supply has been unstable and prices volatile. Vision-language models now extract tables from old scans cheaply, and state surveys are increasingly open to releasing data.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of 15-50k USD per year per company for a basin or state atlas, area-of-interest packs of 5-25k USD, custom data services, and, later, small overriding royalties or success fees on leases won using the data.
non_obvious_insight: The value of data flips when the target commodity changes. A well that reported 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' in 1935 was a dud then, and it is a discovery lead today. Every incumbent data vendor is organized around the old commodity, so nobody re-reads the archive for byproducts. The archives are public and low-margin for the state agencies that hold them, so the moat is the extraction pipeline, cleaning and geological calibration, not data access.
first_30_days: Pick one state survey with well-documented public scans and gas-analysis reports and one target commodity (helium or hydrogen shows are the easiest to demo). Build a proof-of-concept map for one basin using a few thousand well records. Cold-email about 30 junior exploration companies and geothermal developers with the map and one concrete lead they can check. Sell 3-5 area-of-interest packs at around 5k USD each, and ask for pre-payment for the next state.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. title: Replication Bench: Poll-Triaged Experiments With Signed Records

Each job returns a signed record separating protocol, human edits and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). AI-agent customers order the same protocols through an API and can request 'claim-verified' runs before building on a paper.
why_now: There is a large pool of laid-off molecular biologists and postdocs available at near-market rates, seed funds are scrutinizing academic-spinout claims harder, and AI-for-science startups are producing agent-designed experiments faster than anyone can run them.

title: Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics
one_liner: When a US manufacturer leaves a Chinese contract manufacturer, we find out which molds and dies it really owns, and prove whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M revenue) that moved or are moving injection-molded, die-cast, stamped or extruded product out of China within the last 24 months, and hold $200k-$5M of tooling there. problem: Most small and mid-size OEMs cannot say which tools they own, where they physically sit, or what condition they are in. The paper trail is a PO line item from 2016 and a WeChat thread. title: Lab-Sourced Smoke Contamination Benchmark and Loss Index
one_liner: A give-to-get data cooperative that captures post-fire dust wipe, tape lift and air results directly from accredited labs, whoever ordered them. It returns percentile benchmarks to hygienists and adjusters for free, and sells the resulting contamination-prevalence and remediation-cost index to reinsurers, cat modelers, rating agencies and reserving actuaries.
customer: Payers: catastrophe and reserving actuaries at wildfire-exposed carriers, the California FAIR Plan, reinsurance brokers' analytics teams and cat-model vendors, and rating agencies. Contributors, who get the service free: IH firms, public adjusters and 2-3 AIHA-accredited environmental labs. Free-licensed users: DTSC, CDI and LA County, so the index becomes the citable reference.
problem: AB 1795 turns smoke on a standing home into a presumed covered loss with a 30-day clock, yet nobody knows contamination prevalence by distance, home age, construction, HVAC or plume. The only public dataset is EFRU's roughly 50-80 homes (63% elevated lead, one third asbestos, post-remediation). Carrier-vendor data sits in privileged silos. Cat models are built around destroyed structures, and I did not verify whether any vendor has a smoke-on-standing-homes module. Reinsurance and reserving for 2027 must price a blind tail: 13,000+ standing smoke-damage homes in LA alone, with ALE running until clearance. Every hygienist also argues about the comparison basis (urban background dust versus thresholds), and Purdue reports consultants using wrong comparators. No one has a defensible background distribution.
solution: The chokepoint is labs, not reports. Every sample, carrier-side or policyholder-side, runs through a handful of accredited labs. The co-op gives labs a differentiator: a structured electronic data deliverable plus a consent checkbox on the chain-of-custody form ('de-identified results may be contributed to the benchmark'). Contributors get a free percentile report, for example 'kitchen floor wipe lead at the 92nd percentile of 1,400 homes 0.5-1 mile from the perimeter, built 1950-79', plus a neighborhood background-dust distribution that answers the comparator fight. Buyers get a parcel-level contamination probability by contaminant, and an expected remediation-scope and cost distribution calibrated on consenting claims. Delivery is by API, CSV and annual studies, versioned, with a free license to state agencies. Public data (Cal Fire DINS, assessor year built, DTSC soil results) fills the gaps. The model generalizes to CO, OR, HI and any WUI fire.
why_now: The signing of AB 1795 on 9/15/2026 converted smoke from an adjuster judgment into a legislated, presumed, time-boxed loss. Reinsurance and carrier reserving for 2027 must now price the distribution. State standards are two to three years away and the regulators will borrow the largest population dataset available. Labs are commodity businesses hungry for differentiation, and structured data plus LLM tooling makes lab-level ingestion cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $40k-$120k a year per reinsurer, cat modeler or carrier. Bespoke reserving studies at $75k-$150k. A data-processing fee of $15-$25 per sample, paid by labs or contributors, for the percentile reports. A later licensing revenue share with cat-model vendors. Balance-sheet option once the index is trusted: a parametric smoke-remediation trigger calibrated on the co-op's data, built with a licensed MGA and reinsurer capacity. That is a 2029 step and needs admitted-carrier or surplus-lines structuring.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone assumes data comes from adjudicated claims and reports. Labs are the only neutral point that sees both carrier-side and policyholder-side samples, and the percentile report solves the hygienist's biggest weakness, defending the comparison basis, so contributors have a selfish reason to opt in. The hard problem is selection bias: policyholder-side samples skew dirty, and carrier vendors sample thinly and shallowly. The co-op only earns trust if it corrects for who ordered the sample, ideally with at least one carrier's vendor data, or with a randomized sampling frame in one neighborhood. Solving that bias is the scientific moat, and it is exactly what a regulator or actuary will test first.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pitch 3 accredited labs handling fire-zone samples on a consent-based structured feed, aiming for one signed LOI. Request EFRU's dataset and Purdue's reviewed reports under a data-sharing MOU. Days 10-20: assemble the public layer (DINS perimeters and damage inspections, assessor year built, DTSC soil data, CDI task-force figures) and publish a free 'Eaton Fire Smoke Background Dust Benchmark v0' from the EFRU sample (n of roughly 50-100) to seed usage. Days 20-30: sell two paid $15k-$25k 'Smoke Reserving Briefs' to a carrier cat or reserving team and a reinsurance-broker analytics team ahead of renewals. Sign 5 IH firms as contributors. Kill test: if no actuary will pay for a brief built on public and EFRU data, the reinsurer thesis is wrong.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: The co-op sells no assessments and writes no protocol, so HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard, EHS, Home BioTesting and Vert-type firms are contributors and users of the percentile report, not rivals. None can build a neutral cross-vendor dataset because each sees only its own clients, and carrier-vendor data is privileged. EFRU holds about 50-80 homes, does not sell, and is a data partner. Purdue's guidance is method we can cite. IICRC and AIHA publish procedures rather than data. Sedgwick and other TPAs hold claim costs but not lab-grade contamination data and sit on the carrier side. The state will need the data in 2028-29 and is a licensee, not a competitor. Unlike a California-specific protocol that expires when DTSC publishes, the index gets more valuable as standards arrive, because they need a prevalence baseline.

title: Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos
one_liner: A satellite-radar settlement history for every Florida condo tower, sold as the cheap first page of the milestone-inspection and reserve-study file.
