What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: CattleMax, AgriWebb, Gallagher, Merck/Allflex and Vence, HerdDogg, Halter and Ceres Tag are all producer-paid management or hardware tools. A borrower-paid tool sees only what the borrower records, and those vendors cannot audit the customers who pay them. IMI Global's Beef Passport verifies supply-chain claims for a producer-paid program, not cross-counterparty reconciliation or a covenant workflow. We are lender-paid and source-agnostic, and we ingest their CSV exports as just one input, so they become feeders rather than rivals. Their incumbent asymmetry is real: adding lender variance reports means telling their own paying customers they are now audited. The remaining risk is unknown third-party inspection firms, which the interviews must surface, and a possible white-label deal with IMI or an EID vendor.

title: Loss-Draft Clearance Standard for Mortgage Servicers
one_liner: Mortgage servicers and portfolio lenders pay a per-loan fee for verified smoke clearance. That verification gates the final release of insurance loss-draft funds and the end of forbearance on smoke-damaged standing homes. Lenders, not carriers, become the enforcer of a defensible standard.
customer: Loss-draft and disaster-recovery departments at mortgage servicers and subservicers with concentrated Altadena, Pasadena and Palisades books, plus community banks, credit unions and CDFIs around Pasadena and the Westside. Secondary buyers: escrow and title officers on standing-home sales. Homeowners and their PAs are the delivery channel, not the payer.
problem: Servicers hold insurance proceeds on mortgaged, smoke-damaged homes and typically release them in staged draws with a final holdback against completion inspections. For destroyed homes the milestones are objective (foundation, framing). For smoke there is no completion gate: the contractor says 'cleaned', the carrier's vendor says 'clean', and the owner says the house still makes the family sick. EFRU's roughly 50 remediated homes showed 63% with elevated lead and one third with asbestos, so a lender that releases the last draw on an unverified cleaning is funding continued collateral impairment. A servicer that withholds gets complaints and unhappy borrowers paying a mortgage plus rent. I have not verified how servicers handle this today, so this is the riskiest assumption to test first.
solution: A one-page, servicer-adoptable 'Smoke Clearance Acceptance Standard' covering sampling grid, threshold basis, chain of custody and lab accreditation, tied to AB 1795, AIHA and IICRC/RIA/CIRI references and versioned for DTSC's 2028-29 standards. Alongside it, a portal where the borrower's hygienist or remediator uploads results. We verify them (automated checks plus partner CIH-of-record review) and issue a machine-readable Clearance Verification (pass, fail, or specific deficiency list) that the servicer's loss-draft workflow accepts to release the final draw or convert a forbearance. A book-level ledger shows every loan in the burn perimeter, joined to parcels, with status: not tested, tested, remediating, cleared. Testing stays paid by the insurer under AB 1795 or by the borrower from claim proceeds. The servicer pays only for verification and monitoring.
why_now: AB 1795 (effective 1/1/2027) forces insurers to pay for testing and bars ALE termination before clearance, so a verified clearance event now exists in statute and can be a lender milestone. 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage in the LA fires, many mortgaged, are hitting the remediation and final-draw stage through 2027. Meanwhile the state standard will not exist until 2028-29, and servicers adopt vendor standards faster than agencies write them.
revenue_model: Servicers pay $250-$450 per loan verified, usually recoverable as an inspection or protective-advance line they already charge, plus $2-$5 per loan per month for ledger monitoring on flagged loans. Community banks and credit unions pay a flat $15k pilot. Hygienists and remediators can pay $50 to have their evidence pack pre-checked against the standard, since a fail costs them time. Honest sizing: LA alone is roughly 13,000 homes x about 55% mortgaged x $350 x 1.5 verifications, or about $3.7M. The business is the repeatable template for post-disaster loss-draft verification (hurricane mold, flood, wildfire) across the US, not California smoke alone.
non_obvious_insight: The party with real power over whether a smoke repair is 'done' is not the carrier or the state. It is whoever holds the last check. Servicers already control disbursement, already buy standardized inspection work in bulk, and do not need to win the sampling-design argument. They need a pass/fail they can rely on. Lender incentives also align with policyholders (impaired collateral) and with carriers (fewer reopened claims and bad-faith suits), which neutralizes the parent's buyer conflict. If five servicers and credit unions accept the same evidence package, contractors and hygienists will produce to it, so the de facto standard is set by lenders.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ask 5 public adjusters which servicers are sitting on their clients' checks, then hold 25 calls with loss-draft and disaster managers at about 10 servicers and 10 Pasadena-area banks and credit unions. The one question is what evidence would let you release the final draw on a smoke claim. Days 10-20: draft the one-page acceptance standard and get two CIHs and one toxicologist to endorse it publicly. Days 20-30: agree a paid pilot of 15-30 loans at about $300 with one credit union or servicer, and pre-check evidence packs for 10 borrowers referred by PAs. If no servicer says smoke draws are actually stuck, kill or pivot to escrow and title on resale.
lineage: mutation of I0715 ('Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard, EHS, Home BioTesting and Vert-type firms sell assessments to insurers and homeowners and none sells into loan servicing. They become the channel: the ones that produce evidence to our standard win a document lenders accept. Sedgwick and other carrier TPAs are structurally carrier-side, and a lender will not accept a carrier-side attestation as proof of collateral condition. The IICRC and AIHA guides and the Purdue and EFRU resources are cited inside the acceptance criteria, so they are inputs, not rivals. The state's 2028-29 standards make our criteria more specific, not obsolete, because servicers still need a verification workflow. The adjacent risk is property-preservation and loss-draft inspection vendors, who lack IH capability. We would license the standard to them white-label rather than compete.

title: The Reference Panel: Neutral Ruler for E/M Levels
one_liner: A neutral, triple-blind coder-and-physician panel that measures how reliable any E/M level really is, and sells that measurement to scribe vendors, payers and providers who are now fighting over it.
customer: Three sides. First payer: health-system and large-group compliance and counsel with contested encounters (payer record requests, downcode appeals, OIG inquiries). Second: scribe and coding-AI vendors that need independent validation. Third: payers running automated downcoding, which face state laws and regulator scrutiny on human review. Auditors and RCM firms become licensees.
problem: E/M level is a judgment, not a fact. Published studies show weak agreement even among trained coders: one study had five experienced certified coders assign codes to six notes and only one code was unanimous, and another found 36% inter-rater reliability among eight research nurses across 4,137 visits. Yet three AI systems now assign levels (scribes, autonomous coders, payer downcoders) and contradict each other. Each treats its own output as truth, and extrapolated overpayment demands multiply one reviewer's noise across a whole claims universe. Nobody publishes the noise floor, so the dispute goes to whoever has more lawyers.
solution: An independent panel of certified coders plus a physician advisor labels encounters blind against the 2021 MDM and time rules, with adjudication and published agreement statistics (Krippendorff's alpha by specialty and level). An AI pre-read and single coder handle easy cases and only disagreements escalate to a three-person panel, so the average is about 1.6 reviews per encounter. Product ladder: (a) 'Panel-Certified Level' files for contested encounters, giving a level, a confidence and dissent notes, at $60-90 each; (b) annual validation of a vendor's or payer's AI against a held-out panel-labeled set with a published scorecard, $75-200k a year; (c) noise-floor benchmark subscription and consortium membership at $25-50k; (d) later, a licensed evaluator model trained on the adjudicated labels. Governance rules that make it credible: published methodology, physician advisory board, no vendor equity, no single side above 30% of revenue.
why_now: In 2025-26 three sets of AI systems are assigning and contesting E/M levels at scale. Payers' automated downcoding (Cigna's nationwide policy from October 2025) is reported, as are state downcoding laws in Arkansas and Virginia, with more pending. Scribe vendors are advertising 'audit-ready' and 'verified' accuracy. The 'coding arms race' is in the literature. Each side needs a ground truth it can cite, and the trailing 12 months are when disputes and vendor procurement turn to evidence.
revenue_model: Contested-encounter certification at $60-90 per encounter is the first revenue, with cost near $15-25 including adjudication, so about 70% gross margin. Vendor and payer validation at $75-200k a year. Benchmark and consortium memberships at $25-50k a year. Later licensing of the evaluator model. Revenue mix goal is roughly a third from each of providers, vendors and payers to keep neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: The product is the disagreement rate. Once you can say 'certified coders disagree on this specialty's level-4 encounters 30% of the time', a single-reviewer downcode or a single-reviewer audit finding falls inside the noise floor, and an extrapolated overpayment should shrink, which is worth real money to providers. It also turns every incumbent into a customer. VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity, Charta and the AI coders can each validate against or license the panel, so none of them needs to see it as an attack. Credibility is the moat and scales with every adjudicated encounter.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 CPC/CPMA coders and one physician advisor. Approach two health-system compliance teams that have open payer record requests or downcode disputes and offer to triple-blind review 100 contested encounters each at a pilot rate ($8-15k). Publish a 6-page methodology paper and the first anonymized agreement statistics. Offer two scribe or coding-AI vendors a 200-encounter validation on the understanding that results are only published with consent. Aim for one paid pilot and one vendor letter of intent.
lineage: mutation of I0389 ('Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface. | How this version avoids them: It does not compete as another audit platform or AI coder. VMG Health, MDaudit and Healthicity run single-reviewer workflows for one side, so they cannot be neutral, and they are natural licensees and second-opinion buyers. Ambience (95% 'AAPC-verified'), Abridge and DeepScribe self-attest, and the panel is the independent replacement for that claim. Fathom, Arintra and CodaMetrix have the same conflict. Trilliant publishes descriptive studies but has no panel-labeled ground truth. BCBSA and payer AI programs are the counterparty and become customers for calibration. Riskiest assumption is that all sides will accept a neutral panel, which is why the first product is the per-encounter certification that pays before neutrality is proven.

title: Community Lenders Pool Orders to Keep County Appraisers
one_liner: Sell rural credit unions and banks a pooled, multi-year county 'appraisal continuity compact', where their combined order flow plus a fixed capacity retainer makes a retiring appraiser's territory viable for a supervised successor.
customer: Payer: the 4-8 community banks and credit unions that originate mortgages in a rural county cluster whose appraiser is retiring, each paying about $3-8k a year, bought through state credit union leagues, bankers associations and their service arms or CUSOs. Beneficiaries: the retiring appraiser (paid a fixed stipend), a mid-career certified appraiser from an adjacent county acting as supervisor, and 1-2 career-changer trainees (agents, inspectors, adjusters).
problem: A rural lender places 30-100 appraisal orders a year. No single small lender can sustain a trainee, and none is big enough to make an out-of-county appraiser drive 60 miles. When the county's only appraiser retires, orders go to distant AMC panel members, closings slip and purchase loans are lost. Trainee programs like Valligent's assume one lender commits volume. The retiree's book was stable because 15 direct lenders each sent about a dozen orders, so each lender was individually too small to replace it.
solution: 'County Compact': (1) Diagnose at-risk counties by joining board rosters (active certified appraisers and license age) with HMDA originations by lender and county. (2) Sign a 3-year compact among 4-8 lenders in the county: pooled first-look on local orders (lenders still order directly and independently, with no link to value conclusions or loan approval), a turnaround SLA such as 7 business days, and a fixed annual capacity retainer paid to us. (3) Recruit and equip the continuity team: a certified supervisor plus 1-2 trainees, with desk QC and UAD 3.6 tooling. (4) Pay the retiree a fixed 12-month knowledge-transfer stipend for the recorded local-knowledge interview, adjustment grids, neighborhood boundary notes and lender introductions. The retiree does not sign reports and gets no percentage of anything. (5) Give each lender a quarterly turnaround and quality report for their compliance and board files. Money flow: borrower pays the appraisal fee through the lender at the customary fee, 100% to the appraiser firm with no skim or split. Lenders pay us the retainer. We pay the retiree a fixed stipend and the supervisor a per-trainee capacity stipend. Counsel to confirm the retainer is independent of order outcomes and that we stay under state AMC registration thresholds (roughly 15 appraisers per state, to verify) because lenders order directly.
why_now: UAD 3.6 goes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and veterans are choosing to quit. ABA Banking Journal and CSBS have documented rural appraiser shortages in 2026. The AQB exposure draft that drops the college-degree requirement widens the trainee pool. EO 14393 signals regulators want more appraiser supply. State leagues and bankers associations already sell shared services to small members, so the channel exists.
revenue_model: Capacity retainer of $3-8k per lender per year scaled by originations, so about $30k a year for a 6-lender compact, on 3-year terms. Add-on lender-paid collateral QC or desk review at roughly $45 per report. 10% distribution share to the league or CUSO. Rough economics (assumptions): year 1 costs are about $10k retiree stipend, $10k supervisor and trainee capacity stipends and $5k ops and QC, leaving a thin margin. Years 2-3 drop the retiree stipend, giving about 45-50% gross margin at steady state. 50 compacts is about $1.5M a year.
non_obvious_insight: Small lenders are each below the minimum viable volume for any successor, but pooled they equal the retiree's book. The compact re-creates that pool contractually. Lenders are not paying for appraisals, which borrowers still cover, but for the option value of local capacity, priced like a rural fire district. A single delayed or lost purchase loan costs a lender more than its share of the retainer, so 2-3 saved closings a year pay for it. Paying supervisors a capacity stipend funded by the pooled retainer solves supervisor scarcity without taking a cut of trainee fees, so fee-splitting rules are avoided.
first_30_days: Build a county risk map for TX, OH, PA and CO from board rosters and HMDA and NCUA/FFIEC lender lists, and shortlist 15 counties with an aging appraiser and 4+ community lenders. Call appraisal or ordering managers at 20 credit unions and banks and ask which orders were delayed or unplaceable in the last 12 months and what each cost. Offer two state leagues or bankers associations free county risk maps for their members as the door-opener and ask for a pilot. Recruit 2 supervisors and 4 trainees. Get a signed letter of intent for 2 pilot compacts of 3+ lenders each. Commission one counsel memo on appraisal independence and AMC thresholds.
lineage: mutation of I1039 ('Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors. | How this version avoids them: Valligent is national, hires supervisors as employees and relies on a single lender's volume commitment, with no retiree knowledge handoff. This is a county-pooled, multi-lender contract with fixed stipends and no employment. Aloft is a centralized company-appraiser model, not local continuity. Solidifi and AXIS are AMC mentor-matching programs, while this is lender-funded capacity in named counties. PAREA gives experience without supervisors but transfers no local knowledge and does not guarantee anyone orders. Reggora and the AMC consolidators (Class Valuation, Atlas VMS) are platforms and cannot easily offer a multi-lender contractual pool for one county. LIA, OREP and a la mode do not touch this. Fixed stipends and no percentage of trainee or successor revenue avoid the fee-splitting and earn-out legality problems, and the retiree does not need to stay licensed.
